title: Convulsive status epilepticus in a child
stem: Paediatric resus. A 3-year-old girl (about 14 kg) has been fitting for 10 minutes. Her mother says she has had a cold, no previous seizures, and no medicine has been given. She is having generalised tonic–clonic movements now. HR 160, SpO2 90% in air, temperature 38.6 °C.

phases.title: Immediate care
phases.goal: Name it and start the clock; monitor; protect her, airway and oxygen; glucose; access and bloods.

phases.title: Benzodiazepine
phases.goal: Lorazepam for her weight. A second dose if she is still fitting 10 minutes later: two at most.

phases.title: While you wait
phases.goal: A history from her mother; call for help and draw up the second-line drug.

phases.title: Second line
phases.goal: Two doses and still fitting: levetiracetam.

phases.title: After
phases.goal: Recovery position, breathing, the next step, admission; explain to her mother.

events.say: She is still having generalised tonic–clonic movements.
Ten minutes after the lorazepam: still fitting.
Ten minutes after the second dose: still fitting.

review.text: Buccal midazolam dose. Your notes cap it at 5 mg. APLS uses 0.3 mg/kg up to 10 mg.
Second-line drug. Your notes give phenytoin only. Since EcLiPSE and ConSEPT, APLS lists levetiracetam 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) over 5 minutes as first choice or equal to phenytoin.

Second line. APLS (used in Hong Kong paediatrics): levetiracetam 40 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg at about 25 minutes, then the other, then RSI by 45 minutes. AHA/AES: fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam. The script names levetiracetam and phenytoin, which both accept.
Aciclovir dose. BNFc uses 500 mg/m² for 3 months–12 years; many protocols use 20 mg/kg (280 mg here). No Hong Kong paediatric protocol was available to check.

notes:
Checked against the APLS algorithm for convulsive status epilepticus (APLS 7th edition, 2023 update following EcLiPSE/ConSEPT: levetiracetam as a second-line option alongside phenytoin), NICE NG217 (Epilepsies, 2022) and RCUK paediatric guidance.

At 5 minutes: first benzodiazepine — IV/IO lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg), or buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg (max 10 mg) if no access. At 15 minutes (10 minutes later): a second benzodiazepine dose. At 25 minutes: levetiracetam 40 mg/kg (max 3 g) IV over 5 minutes, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes (or phenobarbital 20 mg/kg if already on phenytoin). At 45 minutes: RSI with a senior anaesthetist. Maximum two benzodiazepine doses including pre-hospital doses.

Always check glucose early (treat under 3 mmol/L with 2 mL/kg 10% glucose) and look for the cause (fever, meningitis/encephalitis, electrolytes, trauma, toxins).

Your notes: buccal midazolam max 5 mg (APLS uses 0.3 mg/kg up to 10 mg) and phenytoin as the only second-line drug; APLS now lists levetiracetam first or equally. Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg max 4 mg and PR diazepam 0.5 mg/kg match.

Perfect script checked against an APLS status epilepticus checklist, an AHA/AES checklist, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed every wrong option (restraint, objects in the mouth, wrong doses, a third benzodiazepine). Added: status named, weight said aloud, injury protection stated positively, a history from her mother while waiting, early escalation, aciclovir with ceftriaxone, post-seizure care and the next step, and an explanation to her mother.

Airway: jaw thrust, suction, an oropharyngeal airway if tolerated.

A–B.t: High-flow oxygen, 15 L via a non-rebreather.

D–E.mark: Looks for clues: pupils, fever, rash, injury
D–E.r: Pupils equal and reactive. 38.6 °C. No rash, no sign of injury. "Febrile."

With the cannula: a gas with glucose, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium; FBC, CRP and a blood culture.

opts.t: Mei had a long seizure, probably set off by the fever. The medicine has stopped it. We're treating her in case there's an infection of the brain, and she'll stay in hospital. She'll be sleepy for a few hours.

opts.r: Thank you, doctor. Can I stay with her?
opts.rz: 多謝醫生。我可唔可以陪住佢？

script.say: She's been fitting for 10 minutes: this is convulsive status epilepticus. Note the time and start the clock. Monitoring on, please: ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure. She's 3: (3 + 4) × 2, about 14 kg.

Protect her from injury: clear the space and pad the sides; don't restrain her, nothing in her mouth. Airway: jaw thrust, suction, an oropharyngeal airway if tolerated. High-flow oxygen, 15 litres via a non-rebreather.
Heart rate 160, capillary refill 2 seconds: not shocked. Glucose, please.
Pupils equal and reactive, 38.6 degrees, no rash, no injury: she's febrile.
IV access, please; IO if it's difficult. With the cannula: a gas with glucose, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium; FBC, CRP and a blood culture.
Lorazepam 0.1 mg per kg, 1.4 mg IV. If there were no access: buccal midazolam 0.3 mg per kg, about 4 mg.
Has she had any medicine for this today? Any head injury, or anything at home she could have taken? Has she been unwell? Any seizures before, and are her vaccinations up to date?
script.do: No medicine, no injury; a cold with fever for two days; first seizure; vaccines up to date.

script.say: Please call my senior, the anaesthetist and PICU now: if the second-line drug fails, she'll need RSI. Draw up levetiracetam 40 mg per kg, 560 mg, so it's ready.
Still fitting 10 minutes after the first dose: a second lorazepam, 1.4 mg. That's the limit: two benzodiazepine doses, including any given before hospital.
Still fitting after two doses: second line. Levetiracetam 40 mg per kg, 560 mg IV over 5 minutes; phenytoin 20 mg per kg over 20 minutes is the alternative.
Febrile status: treat for meningitis and encephalitis. Ceftriaxone 80 mg per kg, 1.1 g IV, and aciclovir 20 mg per kg, 280 mg IV over an hour.

Seizure stopped: recovery position, and watch her airway and breathing: respiratory depression after two benzodiazepines. If it starts again: phenytoin 20 mg per kg over 20 minutes, then RSI with the anaesthetist.
Paracetamol for the fever. No lumbar puncture now while she's post-ictal; consider it once she's stable. Admit her to a high-dependency bed under paediatrics, with neuro obs.

Mei had a long seizure, probably set off by the fever. The medicine has stopped it. We're treating her in case there's an infection of the brain, and she'll stay in hospital. She'll be sleepy for a few hours.
